title: Commands and your first session
description: Start in the right place, discover real commands and turn repeated requests into usable workflows.

lessons.title: Open Codex and complete a first read-only task
lessons.goal: Choose the desktop, CLI or IDE surface, sign in, and verify the project before allowing edits.
body: Codex is a coding agent that can inspect files, propose changes and run available tools. Begin with the desktop app when you want projects, chats and previews in one workspace. Current official documentation puts a Codex choice inside the ChatGPT desktop app; ordinary Chat or Work instructions are not automatically Codex instructions. A familiar chat box does not prove that the intended folder is open.

Download the desktop installer through the official download link in the app documentation, follow the normal operating-system installation flow, and sign in through the browser. Choose Codex, then open a disposable project folder. The CLI is a separate terminal client; the IDE extension works beside files in your editor. Local clients support ChatGPT sign-in and supported API-key authentication, with different billing and administration implications. Never paste a key into a practice prompt.

Your first success is a trustworthy description of the environment, not an ambitious generated application. A folder named codex-lab containing a short README is enough. Ask what files and tools are actually visible, then compare the answer with your own file browser. Missing access should be reported as missing. A model cannot verify a project merely from its name or from your account being signed in.
steps: Use the official app instructions for your operating system; if Codex is already installed, inspect it rather than reinstalling.
Create or copy a harmless codex-lab folder with README.md and fictional notes; keep work documents outside the exercise.
Choose Codex and open that folder. In CLI use the intended directory; in IDE confirm the workspace root.
Send the read-only example, open the files it mentions, and correct any mismatch before authorizing a change.

example.label: First app message after opening the returned practice folder
example.code: Read only: confirm the actual working directory. Read README.md, AGENTS.md and notes.json. Report the project purpose, the four note IDs and whether a deployment URL is documented. Inspect whether package.json exists before accepting the README test instruction. Do not edit or install anything.

lessons.exercise: Create a fresh Orbit Notes copy with the lab command and open that exact path in Codex. Ask the first message, compare its four IDs with notes.json, and ask where the application is deployed. Pass only if it identifies the unsupported npm test instruction and reports the deployment address unknown.
checks: The reported working directory matches the folder you opened, rather than an unrelated parent or previous project.
The summary accurately reflects all three facts and identifies the missing information without inventing an answer.
You can explain why the desktop app, terminal CLI and editor extension require different navigation instructions.
mistakes: Opening a broad personal folder and assuming every file inside belongs to this task.
Treating successful sign-in or a polished answer as evidence that the agent inspected the correct project.

sections.title: A first session with a factual answer key
paragraphs: The practice data contains n1, n2, n3 and n4. It is fictional local data; no deployment URL is supplied. README.md recommends npm test, but no package.json exists. A grounded answer distinguishes the project purpose and four records from that unsupported instruction. Do not install a package merely to make the sentence appear valid.

Read notes.json yourself after the response. If the reported directory differs from the returned temporary path, open the right project. A working sign-in proves neither that this folder is selected nor that its contents were inspected.

sections.title: What comes next
paragraphs: Next, choose one small output such as a clearer getting-started document. Name its allowed path, preserve the README as a source, and open the saved result yourself. Installation, authentication, project access and successful delivery are separate milestones; identify which one failed when troubleshooting.

sections.title: Four names you will encounter
paragraphs: A built-in control operates the client, such as opening status or review. A skill packages a repeated workflow in SKILL.md. A plugin distributes skills and tool connections. An MCP server exposes capabilities a client can discover. They are related, but a plugin or server name is not automatically a working slash command.

In the practice project, the README audit is an ordinary request first, then a local readme-check skill. The fictional ticket remains local data unless an actual available connection retrieves a record. Later stations cover plugin distribution and MCP setup; this first exercise establishes which kind of action you are using.

lessons.title: Use built-in commands without guessing
lessons.goal: Find the commands supported by the current client and use them to inspect, steer and review a session.
body: A slash command is a client control typed into the Codex composer, not a shell command and not an ordinary request. In the interactive CLI, type a slash to open the command menu and filter by name. Treat this menu and the current official command reference as the inventory. A command copied from Claude Code, another IDE or an old tutorial is not valid just because its name sounds plausible.

Start with commands that make the session observable. /status displays session settings and context information; /diff shows the working changes, including untracked files; /mcp lists configured external tools. /plan requests planning before implementation, /review examines the working tree, and /new starts a fresh chat. These controls do different jobs: reviewing a diff does not run tests, and starting a new chat does not restore files.

Desktop and IDE menus have their own command and shortcut sets. In the desktop app, the command menu is available through Ctrl+Shift+P or Ctrl+K on Windows, with corresponding Command shortcuts on macOS. Do not assume every CLI slash command appears in every composer. If a control is unavailable, use the documented interface or ask a plain-language question with a concrete output instead of inventing an alias.
steps: Open the CLI slash menu or the desktop command menu and identify three inspection controls that actually appear.
Inspect the session before making a change; record the working folder and the permissions shown by the client.
Make one harmless edit in your scratch project, then use the available diff or review interface to inspect it.
Ask for a short plan for a second task and confirm that planning did not silently become implementation.

example.code: In this disposable copy, change only the README heading to "Heading experiment". Show me that one change in the available review view. I will start a fresh chat next; do not restore or edit any other content.

lessons.exercise: Perform the heading experiment in the linked control notebook. Inspect the changed heading, start a new chat, then read the file again. The diff reflects the harmless edit and you can identify added, removed or unchanged content.
The planned task produces a reviewable plan without modifying the project.
mistakes: Typing /status into PowerShell and expecting the Codex composer to handle it.
Copying Claude-only /rewind or /memory commands and silently assuming Codex has identical behavior.

sections.title: Inspect, steer and reset are different controls
paragraphs: Use the app review view to find the exact heading edit; in CLI, /diff is the corresponding working-change inspection. Neither establishes that any test passed. After starting a new chat, README.md still contains the edit. This observable counterexample is more useful than memorizing that /new resets something.

The linked notebook separates desktop actions, CLI composer controls and operating-system shell commands. Try each separately, record unavailable controls, and compare the actual result. An empty MCP list or absent Git history can be a valid observation.

sections.title: Read the result, not just the command name
paragraphs: A supported command can still have context-dependent behavior. A review may require a Git repository; a tool list may be empty; account restrictions may hide controls. Record the actual result and client version when troubleshooting. Prefer a narrow diagnosis such as “the CLI menu lacks this item” over a global claim that Codex cannot perform the underlying task.

equivalence.summary: Codex has its own current command inventory and desktop shortcuts. Familiar names sometimes overlap with Claude, but their availability and effects must be checked individually.

options: It automatically proves the code is correct.
It restores every modified file.
It helps inspect changes; tests and acceptance remain separate.
quiz.explanation: A diff shows what changed. It does not prove runtime behavior or undo the working tree.

lessons.title: Replace old custom commands with reusable skills
lessons.goal: Recognize deprecated custom-prompt workflows and choose a maintainable Codex skill instead.
body: Repeated requests often begin as saved text: a release-note checklist, a repository orientation prompt, or a review routine. Codex previously supported custom Markdown prompts in the user prompts directory, invoked through a prompts namespace. The current official documentation marks custom prompts as deprecated and recommends skills. Existing prompts are useful migration inputs; their presence does not make them the preferred format for new work.

A skill gives a workflow a name, a description of when it applies, and instructions in SKILL.md. Repository skills live under .agents/skills so a team can version them with the project. Personal skills can live in the user .agents/skills directory. Unlike a saved prompt that must be inserted manually, a skill can support explicit invocation and description-based selection. An accurate trigger matters as much as the instructions.

Migration is a behavioral redesign, not a filename substitution. Remove assumptions about Claude paths, slash namespaces or implicit permissions. Identify the input, permitted actions and concrete output. A skill that drafts release notes should not also create a commit, open a pull request or publish a release unless those actions are part of the current authorization. Review and run the workflow in a scratch project before treating it as reusable.
steps: Choose one saved request that you repeat and describe a successful outcome without relying on its old command name.
List the files or information it consumes, the output it creates, and actions it is not authorized to take.
Draft a skill description that distinguishes a positive trigger from a nearby task that should not activate it.
Test the draft manually with two contrasting requests, then move to the complete skill-creation exercise in the next lessons.

sections.title: A migration changes the workflow contract
paragraphs: The legacy input says review, then asks for npm test, a rewrite and a commit. The starter has no package.json, and a read-only audit should produce findings. The replacement names source files, defines a four-column output and leaves edits for a separately scoped task.

Do not carry Claude-specific argument substitutions, tool front matter or dynamic shell blocks across by analogy. For this instruction-only skill, the target README is ordinary request text. The optional Codex metadata file is a separate documented format; it is unnecessary for this first migration.

sections.title: A small migration is easier to trust
paragraphs: Start with a read-only workflow that returns a document. Add scripts only when deterministic processing is useful. Record which legacy behavior remains and what changes, so reviewers can compare the migration without modifying global configuration.

equivalence.summary: Both ecosystems evolved from custom commands toward skills, but Codex uses its own discovery locations and invocation controls; deprecated /prompts workflows should not anchor new teaching.

quiz.question: What is the recommended starting point for a new reusable Codex workflow?
options: A focused skill with a clear description and SKILL.md.
A new Claude slash-command namespace.
A global script with permission to publish by default.
quiz.explanation: Current Codex documentation recommends skills; their scope should remain proportional to the actual workflow.

lessons.title: Use connected tools without inventing MCP commands
lessons.goal: Translate the idea of a server-backed prompt into a grounded Codex request using available tools.
body: MCP means Model Context Protocol: a server can describe tools and supply information to a client. In the Claude source, some server prompts appear through a special slash-command namespace. That naming scheme is not a general instruction for Codex. Current Codex documentation emphasizes configured servers, tool discovery and natural-language use. Do not promise that a /mcp__server__prompt command will exist in the learner’s session.

In the CLI, /mcp shows the active configured MCP tools; verbose mode can help diagnose a server. In the desktop app, installed plugins and available connections provide the corresponding discovery surface. A listed tool and a working authenticated connection are separate conditions. The server may offer only reads, only certain records, or actions that need approval. A name in a menu is not proof that a requested record can be retrieved.

Build the reusable request around the evidence you need rather than around a guessed tool name. For a ticket summary, specify the ticket identifier, required fields, read-only boundary and source link. If the connection is unavailable, the correct result is an explicit access gap. A sample ticket can support a practice exercise, but it must be labelled sample data and must not be presented as a successful live lookup.
steps: Inspect the current tool inventory in your chosen client and identify one existing read-only connection, if any.
Choose a non-sensitive record you already have permission to view; do not create a new connection for this exercise.
Request a narrow lookup with provenance and instruct Codex to report access failures rather than invent a response.
Compare the returned fields with the original system, or complete the fallback using an explicitly labelled local sample.

example.code: Read exercises/ticket.json in the lab. Return its ID, title, status and source. Label it local fictional data. Then check whether it contains DEMO-999; do not substitute a different ticket or claim an MCP lookup occurred.

The answer distinguishes tool availability, authentication and access to the requested record.
A live response has a source to inspect, or the exercise clearly reports an unavailable connection and sample-only result.
mistakes: Inventing a server or tool name because a tutorial used a similar integration.
Treating permission to read a ticket as authorization to update it or send a message.

sections.title: A missing-record test exposes a false success
paragraphs: The local file contains DEMO-123, Normalize note search, status Open. It has no live source URL and no DEMO-999. Returning DEMO-123 when asked for DEMO-999 fails identifier matching even if the title sounds relevant. The linked guide supplies a complete unavailable-connection answer.

For an already authorized read connection, use the actual returned record and source link, and note the check time. Discover the tool that exists in your session. Claude’s server-prompt namespace is not a Codex API contract; copying it does not create a server or authenticate a request.

sections.title: Reuse the request safely
paragraphs: A skill can later hold this lookup pattern, but authentication stays outside its text. Never embed tokens or passwords. Name the required capability and evidence, then discover the actual tool. Server responses are source material, not authority to expand the task.

equivalence.summary: The Claude lesson exposes MCP prompts as slash commands. This Codex lesson uses verified tool discovery and a capability-based request instead of assuming that namespace is supported.

lessons.title: Create a small project skill
lessons.goal: Build and test an instruction-only skill with a clear trigger and a checkable result.
body: Use a project skill when a workflow has already proved useful through ordinary prompting. For this exercise, a read-only README review is narrow enough to inspect completely. Create a folder under .agents/skills/readme-check in your disposable repository and put SKILL.md inside it. The required metadata is a name and description in YAML front matter, followed by plain instructions.

The description tells Codex when to select the skill; the body explains what to do after selection. Keep those roles distinct. The skill should identify setup claims, compare them with available files, and return a short list of findings. It should neither rewrite the README nor install dependencies merely to make a missing command pass. If evidence is incomplete, a useful finding describes the gap instead of guessing.

Codex detects skill changes automatically, although restarting the client can help when an update does not appear. In CLI or IDE, use /skills or a dollar-prefixed skill mention to select it. The desktop product also exposes a Skills area and selectors; use the invocation offered by that client. Saving a valid file is only a structural milestone. You still need a positive task, an out-of-scope task and a factual result check.
steps: Create only the project-local skill folder in the disposable repository; leave personal and global skill directories untouched.
Save the example as SKILL.md and adapt the description if your real workflow has a narrower trigger.
Invoke it for a README containing one deliberately missing setup instruction, then inspect every reported finding.
Try a request to redesign the UI and confirm this read-only README skill is not used as an implementation workflow.

example.label: Invoke the project skill — CLI or IDE composer
example.code: $readme-check Review README.md against notes.cjs and checks.cjs. Check the npm test claim against actual files. Return a Claim / Evidence / Finding / Suggested correction table. Do not edit files or claim a check ran unless it did.

lessons.exercise: Copy the complete SKILL.md into the fresh practice project and select it through the app skill control. Run the README audit and compare all four findings with the answer key. Inspect file changes to confirm the audit did not edit the project. Try an unrelated implementation request and evaluate whether the description excludes it.
checks: The skill contains a valid name, description and readable instructions at the expected project-local path.
A positive request finds the deliberately unsupported claim and cites actual project evidence.
An unrelated UI request does not inherit the skill’s review-only workflow or gain additional execution permission.
mistakes: Using an attractive name with a description so broad that almost every task matches.
Treating discovery of the skill as proof that its instructions produce accurate results.

sections.title: Judge the skill by findings, not its filename
paragraphs: A correct review identifies unsupported npm test, the raw case-sensitive implementation, and the absent deployment URL. It distinguishes a requirement from an observed capability: the brief requires trimmed, case-insensitive search; notes.cjs does not yet implement it. A table that simply repeats the README misses the planted defect.

The app’s skill selector is the primary path here; CLI and IDE can use the dollar mention. Valid metadata is not proof that the installed client discovered or used the skill. Record selection and output separately, then make a README correction through a new scoped edit request.

sections.title: Keep the first version boring
paragraphs: No script is needed for this exercise. An instruction-only skill is easier to review and travels with the repository without extra runtime dependencies. When a workflow repeatedly needs deterministic parsing, add a small supporting script later and test that script separately. Preserve a clear boundary between the skill being available, being invoked, producing a file and passing a real user review.

sections.title: Optional explicit-only selection
paragraphs: When a workflow must be selected deliberately, the documented Codex agents/openai.yaml policy can set allow_implicit_invocation: false. Create that optional file inside the skill directory only if you choose this behavior; explicit dollar invocation remains available. Keep it separate from Claude’s differently named front matter.

This metadata controls selection, not authorization for commits, messages or publication. The first skill remains instruction-only and read-only. Compare visibility and activation in the installed client rather than treating valid YAML as a successful invocation.

equivalence.summary: The reusable-workflow concept transfers, while Codex requires its own .agents/skills discovery path and supported explicit invocation rather than Claude command syntax.

quiz.question: Which test best demonstrates that readme-check works?
options: Its folder has a professional-looking name.
The YAML parses without an error.
It detects a planted setup mismatch and does not edit the repository.
quiz.explanation: A behavioral test checks both useful findings and the workflow boundary; file validity alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Choose the right control for the task
lessons.goal: Combine natural-language requests, built-in controls and reusable skills without blurring their responsibilities.
body: Use ordinary language to define the result, a built-in control to operate the client, and a skill to apply a repeated workflow. These are complementary tools. A request such as “explain this search and run its existing regression checks” defines work. /diff reveals changes. A project skill can provide a familiar review checklist. Stacking commands and skills without a clear outcome only makes the session harder to understand.

A good task names the relevant input, the allowed scope and an observable finish. In the Orbit Notes practice copy, inspect README.md, AGENTS.md and checks.cjs before asking for a search fix. The exercise brief supplies the real check command because the starter README deliberately contains an unsupported npm test instruction. Reproduce the uppercase and padded-query failures, preserve the supplied checks and unrelated files, and require evidence that the same cases pass after the change. Let Codex choose routine implementation details within that contract.

Keep facts and permissions separate. A README may explain how deployment works, but reading it does not authorize deployment. A review tool may return suggestions, but suggestions do not prove the code was changed. A completed test supports a particular behavior under its tested conditions. Finish with the actual changed files, checks performed, remaining gaps and a preview when the result is visual.
steps: Write the observed problem and a concrete before-and-after example using fictional practice data.
Ask Codex to inspect relevant files and applicable instructions before choosing the smallest useful change.
Use a skill only if its trigger matches; inspect the diff and run the project’s documented relevant check.
Open the actual result, compare it with the requested behavior, and request one specific correction if needed.

Your final inspection distinguishes created, checked and accepted work, with external publication still outside this exercise.
mistakes: Adding repeated instructions to “be perfect” while leaving the expected behavior undefined.

sections.title: Read a real before-and-after result
paragraphs: The unchanged six checks expose two baseline failures: uppercase REVIEW and the padded query. The reference fix computes a trimmed lowercase needle and compares lowercase titles, while filter returns the original objects in their original order. The padded command must print n1: Review launch checklist and n3: Review documentation.

A map-based solution can match the same IDs but copy and lowercase the returned objects. The comparison exercise rejects that candidate through the identity contract. Inspect the implementation and protected files as well as the check summary; correct search IDs alone do not establish preservation.

sections.title: Recover from an unhelpful answer
paragraphs: First identify the missing input or broken assumption. If the wrong directory was inspected, fix the context. If the expected behavior was unclear, supply an example. If the change is correct but the proof is missing, ask for the relevant check. Starting a new chat can reduce clutter, but it does not repair the working tree or replace an evidence-based diagnosis.

title: Project guidance and memory
description: Keep durable instructions explicit and understand what local Codex memories can and cannot preserve.

lessons.title: Separate instructions, chat context and memories
lessons.goal: Put durable project rules in the right place and understand which kinds of context may persist.
body: A chat transcript, project instructions and generated memory solve different problems. The transcript records what happened in one conversation. AGENTS.md states durable working guidance in a file the team can review. Local Codex memories can recall useful context from earlier eligible chats when that feature is enabled. None of these is a complete, continuously updated database of the project’s current truth.

Use AGENTS.md for requirements that must apply, such as the correct test command, boundaries around generated files, or how to preserve another developer’s changes. Keep changing facts in their canonical project documents, not duplicated across every prompt. A remembered test command can become stale after a package migration; the current configuration and relevant project instructions are the evidence to inspect before running it.

Local Codex memory is distinct from ChatGPT web memory and is off by default in current documentation. The desktop setting is Enable Codex memories under Personalization; the CLI exposes chat-level /memories controls when available. The IDE uses its connected host’s memory store. Enabling a feature on one computer does not establish the same state on another host, and generated recall does not replace a saved project artifact.
steps: List one durable team requirement, one changing project fact and one temporary task decision from your scratch project.
Assign the requirement to AGENTS.md, the fact to a canonical document, and the temporary decision to the current task context.
Inspect whether memory controls are available in your chosen client without changing their current setting.
Ask Codex to identify the source of each relevant claim and recheck any memory-derived fact against the current files.

Changing facts are checked against current evidence and stale recall is not presented as confirmed.
You distinguish the local host’s memory controls from ChatGPT web settings and from this website’s course progress.
mistakes: Putting passwords, customer records or one-time instructions into a reusable project-guidance file.
Assuming a generated memory is current, complete, or available in every client and on every machine.

sections.title: Context classification has a falsifiable result
paragraphs: The rule to preserve WORK-NOTE.md belongs in AGENTS.md. The current count comes from notes.json. The old 4-pass/2-fail result describes the baseline and can become stale immediately after a fix. A request to return only an outline belongs to the current task unless deliberately saved as continuing guidance.

The linked ledger supplies all four cases and a stale-result counterexample. A fresh conversation should be given the task goal and relevant checkpoint; it should not promote every past decision into a permanent rule. Optional memory can locate evidence, but the exercise works without it.

sections.title: A useful source-of-truth habit
paragraphs: Give each important fact one maintainable home. Reference that file when a task needs it instead of copying its contents into several instruction layers. When two sources disagree, identify their scope and dates before choosing which applies. For example, a recent package script can invalidate an old setup note, but it does not silently authorize a deployment that the current task never requested.

equivalence.summary: Claude’s CLAUDE.md and auto-memory model are replaced by Codex AGENTS.md guidance plus a separate, optional host-local memory system with its own controls.

quiz.question: Where should a team’s mandatory test command primarily live?
options: Only in the agent’s generated memories.
In reviewed project guidance or checked-in documentation.
Only in a chat that one person remembers.
quiz.explanation: Mandatory guidance needs an explicit, reviewable source. Memory is an optional recall layer, not the only home for a rule.

lessons.title: Initialize useful project guidance
lessons.goal: Create a concise AGENTS.md grounded in the repository, then verify that a fresh session reads it.
body: AGENTS.md is a plain Markdown file for instructions that should outlive one conversation. The CLI /init command generates a starting scaffold in the current directory. In the desktop app or IDE, you can also ask Codex to draft project guidance from the files it inspects. This is a writing task with consequences: an inaccurate instruction can be repeated in every later task, so the generated draft needs review.

Begin with facts visible in the scratch repository. Identify the project purpose, the documented run and test commands, and the files that should not be modified routinely. If a command is absent, record the gap instead of adopting a familiar npm script. Add a small working agreement about checking results and preserving unrelated changes. A short accurate file is more useful than a long generic engineering policy.

Inspect any existing AGENTS.md before generating or replacing it. There may already be important local rules or another contributor’s changes. In this lesson, create guidance only inside the disposable practice project and leave your Codex home untouched. Once the file is reviewed, start a fresh session in that project and ask which instruction sources loaded. Discovery happens at session startup, so a stale session is a poor test of a newly written file.
steps: Confirm the scratch project root and check whether AGENTS.md or AGENTS.override.md already exists there.
Read README.md and the actual project configuration; distinguish verified commands from plausible but untested suggestions.
Use CLI /init, or ask for a project-local draft, then edit the result to remove unsupported claims and broad permissions.
Start a fresh session and request an instruction-source summary before delegating a small practice task.

After review, integrate into AGENTS.md and start a fresh session at the intended project. Ask for loaded source paths and the test command. In the optional CLI track /init generates a scaffold inside the current directory. It is a composer control, not a terminal command or proof that the scaffold’s assertions are true.

sections.title: Review guidance like code
paragraphs: Read each sentence as a future instruction. Replace vague demands with observable expectations and verify commands against the repository. Keep task authority separate from build documentation. Improve the smallest relevant guidance file instead of duplicating policies globally.

lessons.title: Understand the AGENTS.md instruction chain
lessons.goal: Predict which global, repository and nested instruction files apply to a specific working directory.
body: Codex discovers instructions in a defined chain when it starts. At the global layer, it looks in the Codex home directory, normally .codex in your user home. It prefers a nonempty AGENTS.override.md over AGENTS.md there. At project scope, it walks from the project root toward the current working directory and selects at most one instruction file at each directory level.

Within a directory, the order is AGENTS.override.md, AGENTS.md, then configured fallback filenames. More specific files appear later in the combined instructions and can refine earlier guidance. An override in one directory does not mean that every parent instruction disappears: it replaces the ordinary file selected at that same directory. Keep specialized instructions close to the work they govern rather than changing the global layer for a single project.

This mechanism depends on the actual working directory and project root. A file sitting in a sibling folder is not automatically the governing source for your session. Instruction size is also bounded; the documented combined default limit is 32 KiB. When guidance looks wrong, inspect the selected path and override files, then restart in the intended directory. Do not try to solve discovery problems by repeatedly pasting conflicting instruction copies into chat.
steps: Draw the path from your scratch repository root to a nested docs folder, marking every applicable instruction file.
Predict which file is selected at a directory containing both AGENTS.md and AGENTS.override.md.
Start a fresh session at the root, then another in docs, and ask for the loaded source paths and applicable differences.
Compare the predictions with the evidence; correct the folder or file placement before editing any configuration defaults.

mistakes: Assuming every AGENTS.md anywhere in the repository loads into every chat.
Confusing config.toml precedence with Markdown instruction discovery; they are related configuration mechanisms with different purposes.

sections.title: Test the override and its absence
paragraphs: The fixture includes root AGENTS.md, ordinary docs guidance, a docs override and contradictory sibling guidance. At docs, the expected project chain retains the root preservation rule and selects the docs override’s short-heading rule. The ordinary docs file and sibling file are counterexamples: neither should be selected at that level.

Remove the override only in the disposable exercise and start a new docs session. The ordinary docs rule should now apply. Compare actual loaded paths, not just a fluent summary. The offline verifier checks these fixture files; it does not claim to have executed Codex discovery.

sections.title: Resolve conflicts explicitly
paragraphs: If two instructions appear incompatible, name the files, scopes and concrete conflict. A local test command can refine a root command for a specialized service, but it should not erase unrelated requirements. Put the resolution in the smallest maintainable source when you are authorized to edit it. For a shared repository, preserve existing agreements and ask about a material unresolved conflict instead of silently choosing whichever sentence is easiest to follow.

equivalence.summary: The hierarchical idea transfers from Claude memory, but Codex has explicit AGENTS.override.md selection, root-to-working-directory discovery and its own size/configuration limits.

lessons.title: Split modular guidance from execution rules
lessons.goal: Organize project-specific instructions without confusing documentation rules with sandbox command policy.
body: The word rule can refer to two different things. A prose rule might say how to write a changelog; an execution rule controls whether a command can run outside the sandbox. The Claude source uses modular Markdown rules, including path-specific metadata. Codex does not inherit that .claude/rules format simply because the repository contains it. Use documented Codex instruction discovery and explicit references instead.

For modular guidance, keep AGENTS.md short and point to a focused document when a task needs it. A UI guideline file can explain naming, accessibility and visual checks without loading a long design policy into every unrelated task. Nested AGENTS.md files can specialize guidance by working directory. A reference is a reading instruction, not a guarantee that arbitrary linked Markdown has already been loaded automatically.

Codex execution rules are a separate, currently experimental feature using .rules files and prefix_rule entries. They match command argument prefixes and return allow, prompt or forbidden decisions. When several rules match, the most restrictive decision wins. Project-local rule layers require project trust. Do not put stylistic preferences in that file type or treat an allow decision as user authorization to send, publish or alter an external system.
steps: Classify three proposed rules as project guidance, optional reference material or command execution policy.
Move a detailed documentation convention into docs/writing-guidelines.md in the scratch project.
Reference that file from project guidance only for documentation tasks, then ask Codex to confirm what it actually read.
Read the execution-rule example as a draft only; leave personal policies and trusted-project settings unchanged.

example.label: A modular reading instruction in project AGENTS.md
example.code:
## Documentation work
Before editing documentation, read docs/writing-guidelines.md.
Use that file for heading and example conventions.
For code-only tasks, read it only when the task also changes public documentation.
Preserve unrelated edits and report the actual validation performed.

checks: The modular guideline is explicitly referenced and its use is verified through an actual documentation task.
No unsupported Claude YAML path-rule syntax is presented as a Codex instruction mechanism.
You can distinguish prose guidance, command policy and user authorization with a concrete example of each.
mistakes: Copying .claude/rules files unchanged and assuming Codex interprets their metadata.
Allowlisting a broad shell prefix to make a writing convention easier to follow.

sections.title: A concrete policy result without installing a rule
paragraphs: The supplied review.rules prompts for the prefix node --test and forbids the narrower node --test private-checks.cjs. The two evaluator examples show why the stricter matching decision wins. The file lives outside active .codex/rules locations; evaluating it does not grant permission or run checks.cjs.

For the writing exercise, keep the convention in Markdown and reference docs/writing-guidelines.md from AGENTS.md. Correct the unsupported README command, label it unrun until executed, and compare the resulting document. Prose instructions and execution-policy syntax solve different problems.

sections.title: An execution rule is not a style rule
paragraphs: If you later need command policy, study the official prefix matching and test tools before installing a rule. A harmless-looking command wrapper can contain more than one action, so broad exceptions require care. This beginner exercise deliberately changes only project documentation. It teaches the distinction without weakening the learner’s sandbox or modifying personal command approvals.

equivalence.summary: Claude modular Markdown rules are adapted through Codex nested guidance and explicit reference documents; Codex .rules files are a distinct command-policy feature, not a matching prose-rules system.

quiz.explanation: A writing convention is prose guidance. Execution policy and credentials serve different purposes.

lessons.title: Use local memories with provenance and limits
lessons.goal: Understand optional Codex memory generation, inspect the controls and verify recalled facts before relying on them.
body: When enabled, local Codex memories can turn useful context from eligible earlier chats into generated files for future work. Current documentation says the feature is off by default. Memories are produced in the background after a chat has been idle long enough; active or short-lived sessions may be skipped, and generation can pause near usage limits. “We discussed it” is therefore not evidence that a durable memory already exists.

The desktop app offers machine-level controls under Settings, Personalization, including Enable Codex memories and a choice about memories from tool-assisted chats. The /memories command controls whether the current chat uses existing memories or can contribute to future memory generation. Those chat choices do not change global settings. CLI and IDE behavior follows the connected Codex host; ChatGPT web memory is a separate system.

Generated state lives under the Codex home memories directory and can be inspected when troubleshooting. Do not make manual edits there your primary control surface. Keep mandatory project rules in AGENTS.md and important deliverables in canonical project files. Memory can help you find earlier evidence, but a recalled path, package version or business fact may be stale. Recheck the actual source before a consequential decision or action.

title: Checkpoints, recovery and Git
description: Separate conversation history from file state, inspect changes and practise bounded recovery.

lessons.title: Know what a checkpoint actually protects
lessons.goal: Separate conversation recovery, local file recovery and external side effects before experimenting.
body: A checkpoint is useful only when you know which state it captures. The Claude source describes automatic snapshots with a dedicated rewind interface. Do not transfer that promise to Codex. In Codex, a saved chat preserves conversation history, a Git commit preserves selected repository files, and a backup preserves whichever files were actually copied. These mechanisms overlap only partly and must be evaluated separately.

Before a change, identify three state boundaries: the chat, the working files and external systems. Starting or forking a chat can change the conversation context without reverting files. Restoring a file through Git does not erase the conversation that discussed it. An email, published release or database change cannot be undone merely by returning to an earlier chat message. Plan recovery around the actual resource being changed.

The official CLI guide recommends Git checkpoints before and after tasks. In a practice project, inspect the starting state, preserve unrelated work and use a small baseline commit or separate copy. Record the command needed to check behavior. This makes experimentation measurable: you can compare the baseline and candidate, rather than relying on a vague recollection that the project seemed to work before.
steps: Choose one harmless local task and list the conversation, files and external resources it might affect.
Inspect existing changes, then make a baseline commit or separate copy only after identifying the intended files.
Record a small behavior check and its starting result before asking Codex to make the experimental change.
Inspect the candidate and decide whether to keep, refine or restore the affected files using the recorded baseline.

example.label: Ask for a recovery plan before a local experiment
example.code: Before changing this scratch project, inspect its current state and identify unrelated edits. Explain what protects the chat history, the files and any external state. Propose a small file baseline and a behavior check. Do not claim a chat fork restores files, and do not run a destructive reset or contact external services.

lessons.exercise: Create a fresh practice copy and record its actual path and baseline check. Change only the README heading in that copy, keeping the original starter untouched. Identify how you would recover the file and where conversation history lives. Explain what this copy does not capture: later untracked files and any external system.
checks: You can name exactly what the baseline captures and which untracked or external data it does not protect.
A behavior or content check exists before the experiment, so the candidate can be compared meaningfully.
The recovered file matches the baseline and unrelated work remains intact.
mistakes: Treating a saved chat as a complete filesystem snapshot with universal undo.
Starting an experiment before checking whether another person already has uncommitted changes in the project.

sections.title: Name the protected content before experimenting
paragraphs: The supplied starter copy is a concrete baseline: you can open it and compare the candidate. An optional staged Git tree protects eight named starter paths for this exercise. Neither is an automatic Codex snapshot of the conversation, machine, ignored files or external services.

Use the recovery guide to make a deliberate heading experiment, then inspect the resulting file. A new chat changes context; it does not restore the heading. The useful later paragraph in the next exercise makes whole-file restoration an observable loss counterexample.

sections.title: Small experiments reduce recovery cost
paragraphs: A focused change to one document is a better first exercise than a broad refactor. Keep generated files, local configuration and external actions outside the initial experiment. If the task later needs a database migration or publication, design a separate recovery procedure for that system. A checkpoint label is not a guarantee of transactional rollback across every connected tool.

equivalence.summary: Codex is taught through explicit Git/file baselines and saved chats, rather than promising the Claude automatic checkpoint-and-rewind system or its retention behavior.

quiz.question: Forking a chat is sufficient to undo which of these automatically?
options: Every file written after the fork point.
A message already sent to an external service.
Neither; conversation branching alone establishes no file or external rollback.
quiz.explanation: A fork copies conversation history. File and external-state recovery require their own verified mechanisms.

lessons.title: Find the evidence needed for recovery
lessons.goal: Use Codex review views and Git inspection to identify the actual baseline and changed files.
body: The source lesson opens a dedicated checkpoint browser. In Codex, begin with the evidence your client actually offers: saved chats, the review panel and the repository’s version history. The desktop app documents a review-tab shortcut, including Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows. The CLI /diff command displays working changes. Neither interface should be described as a browser of guaranteed automatic file snapshots.

A useful recovery inspection answers what changed, which files belong to the experiment, and which baseline you intend to restore. Git status distinguishes tracked edits and untracked files; a normal git diff does not display an untracked file’s content. Codex /diff is documented to include untracked files, but you should still inspect their paths and contents. Do not let a clean-looking partial diff hide a newly generated file.

A chat transcript adds intent and tool history, while repository history adds file versions. Compare both when a change appears unexpected. A commit timestamp alone does not prove that all relevant files were included. The linked Orbit Notes --git copy deliberately uses a staged index baseline and has no HEAD commit: inspect it with git show :README.md. In a different repository with a verified commit, git show HEAD:README.md and git log inspect that committed history instead. Record the actual baseline type rather than assuming those commands are interchangeable.
steps: Create the lab’s fresh Git-enabled copy from the course folder with node labs/project-workflow/create-workspace.cjs --git, if Git is already available; then open its returned path in Codex.
Run the read-only commands below inside that exact practice directory, and inspect untracked files separately.
Inspect the staged README baseline and current working file before proposing restoration; use a separate known-good copy if Git is unavailable.
Write a recovery note naming the target files, the index tree or recovery copy, preserved unrelated work, and the check to run afterward.

sections.title: Read the index, worktree and untracked output separately
paragraphs: In this no-commit teaching repository, AM README.md means the file is added in the index and modified in the worktree. The untracked notes-draft.md appears as ??. git diff -- README.md compares the working candidate with the index; it does not include the draft’s contents. Open that file separately.

git show :README.md reads the staged version. git show HEAD:README.md cannot read a commit that does not exist here. The linked exercise records these real states and makes the baseline type explicit, so missing HEAD is understood rather than addressed through identity or remote changes.

sections.title: When Git is unavailable
paragraphs: Use a separate known-good copy and compare the named file directly in an editor. Record that the exercise used a copy rather than pretending a commit exists. Do not install Git or alter global settings just to complete this inspection. The same reasoning applies: establish the source of the baseline, include newly created files in the inventory and preserve any work outside the experiment.

lessons.title: Choose between chat reset and file restoration
lessons.goal: Select a recovery action that matches the problem, preserving unrelated work and verifying the outcome.
body: The Claude source offers distinct rewind choices for conversation and code. Codex has different documented controls. /new starts a fresh CLI chat, /resume reloads a saved chat, and /fork creates a new chat from history. The desktop’s Undo last app action shortcut is documented, but that wording does not establish a complete rollback of arbitrary files, shell commands or external actions. Use only the behavior you can verify.

If the conversation is confused but the files are correct, start a fresh task with a compact factual handoff. If the files are wrong, inspect their diff and restore only the intended content from a known baseline. Those are different operations. You may keep the full conversation for diagnosis while reverting a local document, or keep a correct implementation while abandoning an unhelpful chat direction.

File restoration can discard work, so first identify and preserve changes outside the experiment. The linked Orbit Notes exercise requires a targeted heading correction while retaining a useful later paragraph; a whole-file restore does not meet that requirement. In a separate case where every working edit to the named tracked file is deliberately rejected, git restore --worktree -- README.md restores the lab’s staged index version. A verified committed baseline can be selected with --source=HEAD only when HEAD actually exists. Neither operation removes new untracked files or reverses remote effects.
steps: Classify the problem as incorrect conversation context, incorrect local files or an external action needing separate handling.
Inspect the baseline and current diff, and preserve any unrelated edits before choosing the recovery action.
For this heading-only Orbit Notes exercise, correct just the rejected heading in the current README; retain the useful paragraph and avoid whole-file restoration.
Recheck the recovered behavior and add a factual handoff if a new chat will continue the task.

The useful paragraph and unrelated edits survive the recovery.

mistakes: Using a repository-wide hard reset for a single rejected edit.
Assuming Ctrl+Z, /new or /fork provides the same recovery guarantees as Claude’s rewind menu.

paragraphs: Keep the corrected check command and append Useful review: preserve this paragraph. Then reject the heading experiment. The wanted document has the original Orbit Notes heading, corrected node command and later paragraph. A targeted heading edit achieves all three.

In a different disposable copy, whole-file restoration from the index removes both unstaged improvements and leaves the untracked draft untouched. The offline verifier executes both transformations and compares actual content. It does not emulate a Codex rewind or claim that chat history changes file state.

sections.title: The narrowest successful recovery
paragraphs: A small corrective edit can preserve more useful work than whole-file restoration. Inspect its diff and keep a recovery copy if needed. For external effects, use the affected system’s supported correction process within the current authorization.

equivalence.summary: Claude’s code/conversation rewind options are mapped to separate Codex chat controls and explicit file-level recovery; no identical checkpoint restore promise is made.

quiz.question: You want to reject one heading change while retaining a useful new paragraph. What is best?

quiz.explanation: A targeted correction preserves the useful work; a whole-file restore or broad reset can discard more than intended.

lessons.title: Experiment with branches, forks and small checks
lessons.goal: Compare two implementation approaches without confusing their conversations, checkouts or evidence.
body: A useful experiment has a question, a baseline and a decision criterion. “Try another approach” is incomplete unless you know what to compare. In Orbit Notes, compare two implementations of searchNotes in notes.cjs against the same uppercase, whitespace, substring and object-preservation checks. One approach can filter the original objects; another can copy and lowercase every returned note. Both may appear to solve search, yet only one preserves the stated identity contract. The method should produce evidence that helps choose, not merely two different summaries.

A Codex chat fork preserves a conversation branch. A Git branch or worktree separates repository work in a different way. Current CLI documentation supports managed worktrees for suitable new or forked local tasks, but a chat fork in the same checkout can still affect the same files. Before parallel implementation, identify which checkout each task edits. Read-only exploration can share a project more easily than simultaneous edits.

Keep the experiment small enough to inspect and reverse. Save a baseline, give both candidates the same input and run the same relevant checks. Do not merge both solutions merely because both produced plausible summaries. Decide using behavior, simplicity and maintenance implications. A passing test is useful evidence, but the final result still needs a human-readable diff and an explanation of what the test does not cover.
steps: Write one comparison question and an acceptance example before creating another chat or checkout.
Preserve the baseline and decide whether the candidates need separate working directories to avoid file conflicts.
Ask for two bounded approaches, recording the checkout and changed files for each candidate.
Run the same checks, inspect the diffs and keep one result through an explicit, reviewable integration step.

example.label: An experiment brief with a real decision criterion
example.code: Compare two small approaches to searchNotes in the disposable Orbit Notes lab. Read README.md, AGENTS.md and checks.cjs; reproduce the baseline with node --test checks.cjs. Keep edits in separate verified copies, or compare plans read-only if isolation is unavailable. Evaluate both with the unchanged six checks and node cli.cjs "  REVIEW  ". Preserve source data, tests and unrelated work. Recommend one implementation with file evidence; do not merge or publish automatically.

lessons.exercise: Create two separate Orbit Notes practice copies from the same supplied starter. Compare a query-normalizing filter that returns original note objects with a copy-and-normalize approach. Run the same six checks in both directories and record their actual paths. Choose the implementation using search behavior, input identity and order, then inspect its diff. If you cannot run code, compare two README outlines in separate files and explicitly mark behavior checks unrun.
checks: Both candidates begin from the same verified baseline and are judged against the same task requirements.
You can identify each candidate’s conversation and actual filesystem location without assuming they are the same thing.
The selected result has an inspected diff, comparable checks and a clear reason for the decision.
mistakes: Forking two chats into the same checkout and assuming their concurrent edits are isolated.
Changing the evaluation cases for the preferred candidate and calling the comparison fair.

sections.title: A comparison whose losing candidate is plausible
paragraphs: Both supplied implementations normalize the query and match n1/n3. Candidate A filters the original objects; candidate B maps them to new objects with lowercased titles. Running the unchanged checks in two fresh directories gives A six passes, B five passes and one identity failure. Inspect the actual query text too: B alters the displayed titles.

This distinguishes search matching from the preservation contract. A chat fork branches conversation; the two actual temporary directory paths establish file isolation here. Keep the losing result as evidence, then choose the simpler contract-preserving implementation.

sections.title: Prefer sequential experiments when isolation is unclear
paragraphs: Parallel work is an option, not a prerequisite. If the client cannot establish separate checkouts or the task is tiny, test candidate A, preserve its diff, restore the verified baseline and test candidate B. Record the sequence and keep the evidence. This often gives a beginner a clearer comparison than coordinating several active agents with uncertain file ownership.

equivalence.summary: The source’s save/rewind/try-again pattern is preserved through explicit baselines and isolated or sequential Codex experiments rather than automatic rewind snapshots.

options: Whenever the conversation has a new name.

Whenever the agent says the approaches are different.

lessons.title: Use Git checkpoints as durable file evidence
lessons.goal: Create a small reviewable baseline, inspect the candidate and distinguish version history from chat history.
body: Git records versions of selected files. A commit is useful because it identifies content you can inspect later, independently of a chat interface. It does not automatically include every file in the folder, preserve ignored outputs or snapshot an external service. Before calling a commit a recovery point, verify which files it contains and whether the working tree already had changes that must be preserved.

The default Orbit Notes --git setup stages the named starter files and records an index tree without creating a commit. It is a useful comparison baseline, but not durable history. The separate verify-commit demonstration creates a fresh owned repository and two actual commits using fictional author identity only for those invocations; it does not save identity settings or use a remote. In your own real repository, use its normal reviewed Git workflow and author identity instead of copying this fictional practice identity. Neither exercise requires changing global Git configuration.

After the Codex task, compare the working tree with the baseline and run the relevant project check. The chat explains the intent; the diff shows file changes; the check supplies behavior evidence. A later commit can preserve the accepted candidate, but committing is not the same as customer acceptance or deployment. Keep those milestones separate so a clean repository does not become a misleading claim that all work is finished.
steps: Create a fresh Orbit Notes --git copy using the linked lab guide, inspect its actual path and review every staged file.
Use the staged index tree for the exercise and identify it explicitly; choose a separate copy if Git is unavailable.
Complete the focused task and compare its working files with that index baseline and the original six-check contract.
Record the actual index tree or copy, relevant check results, and untracked/ignored outputs. Treat a later commit only as a separate optional step with an already usable identity.

sections.title: Create and inspect a real practice commit
paragraphs: The separate verifier creates two actual commits only inside its newly owned temporary repository. Fictional author identity and disabled signing are invocation-only Git options; no identity settings are saved. The first commit deliberately records the broken starter, and the second records only the focused README and search fix.

Inspect the returned path, commit IDs, git ls-tree --name-only HEAD and git show HEAD:README.md. The draft stays untracked. A later README paragraph stays unstaged and is absent from HEAD. This makes history concrete while retaining the index-only default for earlier recovery exercises.

paragraphs: The optional setup stages .gitignore, AGENTS.md, README.md, WORK-NOTE.md, checks.cjs, cli.cjs, notes.cjs and notes.json. Inspect the actual staged list and tree identifier. Later git add changes the index; the exercise calls it a disposable comparison baseline, not durable commit history.

After the candidate, inspect the working diff and untracked draft separately. The offline demonstration restores one file from the index and confirms the draft survives. A real reviewed commit records selected content in history, but it still does not include untracked/ignored material or prove deployment, user acceptance or external rollback.

sections.title: Git and Codex have complementary roles

lessons.title: Understand the interactive CLI and scripted runs
lessons.goal: Choose the terminal workflow that fits the task and confirm its environment before running work.
body: The command-line interface lets Codex work from a terminal against local project files. Running codex opens an interactive terminal user interface, often shortened to TUI. You can give an initial request and continue with follow-ups, inspect commands and steer the task. The desktop app is still the default learning surface for this course; use the CLI when terminal navigation or repeatable execution makes the work easier.

A scripted run uses codex exec rather than Claude’s print-mode flags. It accepts a task and finishes without opening the interactive conversation UI. This is useful for a bounded summary or structured extraction. It is not automatically safe because it lacks a chat window: the working directory, authentication, permissions and available tools still determine what the agent can do. Begin with a read-only task that produces an inspectable result.

Install through an option documented on the official Codex CLI page if the CLI is absent, using your normal software-approval process. The current guide includes standalone installation for supported operating systems and package-manager alternatives. This course does not run installation for you. If the CLI is already available, check its version and help rather than installing another copy. Multiple installations can make documentation and observed behavior disagree.

paragraphs: Your shell’s current directory matters just as much as the folder selected in the app. Quote paths containing spaces and confirm whether commands run on the local computer, a remote host or a container. If a scripted run refuses a non-Git folder, use an appropriate disposable Git project rather than disabling repository checks casually. An environment mismatch should be diagnosed before model settings are changed.

lessons.title: Navigate the CLI command families
lessons.goal: Use help, authentication checks, session continuation and review commands without mixing shell and composer syntax.
body: The shell command codex can launch several workflows. Some commands inspect the local setup, some start work and others change saved state. Begin with help at the relevant level: codex --help for the command family and codex exec --help for a scripted run. A command that authenticates, installs a plugin or deletes a session is not equivalent to a read-only inventory command.

Useful inspection controls include codex --version and codex login status. The latter reports whether credentials are present; that does not prove access to every model, workspace or connected record. codex resume opens saved interactive sessions, while codex fork creates a new chat from a saved session. Confirm the working directory when resuming, especially if the current terminal folder differs from the session’s saved project.

For a repository review, codex review --uncommitted selects uncommitted changes as the target. Review findings still need evaluation and relevant tests. Inside the TUI, slash controls such as /status and /diff operate the live session; they are not external shell executables. Keeping a small notebook of command, location and effect prevents accidental execution of a state-changing operation while you were only trying to inspect something.

sections.title: A saved session is not a restored repository

Inspect the working folder before accepting either selection. In the practice project, starting a new chat leaves a changed README heading unchanged.

A review examines the chosen diff and returns findings; it does not imply fixes were applied. For scripted continuation, codex exec resume --last chooses recent history associated with the directory. Deliberately select a harmless practice session and check installed help rather than relying on an unknown last task.

sections.title: Read-only diagnostics can still contain sensitive details
paragraphs: A diagnostic report may reveal local paths, account context or configuration even when it does not edit anything. Inspect such output before sharing it and never paste authentication files into a support request. This lesson does not require logout, deletion, plugin installation or remote-control setup. Use the smallest command family that answers the current question and preserve the result with its project and client context.

lessons.title: Set scope with deliberate CLI flags
lessons.goal: Choose a working directory and permissions for one run without casually weakening persistent configuration.
body: Flags configure a particular invocation. The most useful beginner controls identify where the task runs and what filesystem access it needs. --cd selects the working directory; --sandbox read-only prevents the agent’s ordinary sandboxed workflow from editing project files. For work that needs changes, the documented workspace-write mode is more appropriate than a broad full-access default. Inspect actual client help because flags and policies evolve.

Approval policy and sandbox scope answer different questions. The sandbox constrains the environment; approval policy determines when the agent requests authorization for eligible actions. A prompt that says “do not edit” communicates intent but does not replace those controls. Conversely, permission to write inside a folder does not authorize publishing a site or sending messages through an external integration. Tool-specific permissions may need separate consideration.

Current configuration precedence gives CLI flags and one-off configuration overrides priority over ordinary defaults, while managed requirements can still constrain allowed behavior. Personal defaults, trusted project configuration and profiles have their own layers. Do not edit global settings to solve a one-run need. The old --full-auto flag is no longer supported in current documentation, so tutorials should use explicit current settings rather than preserve obsolete convenience switches.

sections.title: A wrong-directory counterexample is more than a flag list
paragraphs: The two fixtures deliberately disagree. Compare the planned working directory with the source, then validate the red answer against the blue README to see a factual failure. This exposes correct-looking output carried from an earlier workspace into the current task.

The optional capture uses --sandbox read-only and --ask-for-approval never so a needed escalation fails rather than silently widening the run. The host process writes reports into a fresh temporary directory. These are invocation choices, not persistent Codex setting edits. Review current help and managed constraints before a real run. The global approval flag precedes exec in the supplied runner; an exec-local placement is rejected by the checked client. Its explicit repository-check exception applies only to the known read-only fixture folders.

sections.title: A read-only agent is not a read-only shell
paragraphs: If you redirect output with your shell or use a client output-file option, that surrounding process may create a report even when the agent’s project sandbox is read-only. Name the output deliberately and do not overwrite an important source. Evaluate the whole command you are running, including redirection and pipelines, rather than checking only the sandbox flag in the middle.

lessons.title: Capture final answers and structured events
lessons.goal: Choose human-readable, JSON Lines or schema-constrained output and validate the actual files produced.
body: A scripted task can produce several kinds of output. In ordinary codex exec mode, progress goes to stderr while the final agent message goes to stdout. That distinction helps when a shell saves a report. The --output-last-message option, also available as -o, saves the final answer to a named file. Choose a new report path rather than redirecting into a source file you meant only to inspect.

With --json, stdout becomes a stream of JSON Lines events: each line is a separate JSON object describing progress or an item. This is not one large JSON document and not necessarily just the final answer. A consumer must parse each line and distinguish completion from failure. Saving a final message alongside an event stream gives you both an inspectable summary and execution evidence without confusing their formats.

For a stable machine-readable final result, --output-schema requests a response shaped by a JSON Schema. The schema constrains structure, not factual truth. A project name can satisfy a string field while still being invented. Include a way to report unknown information, compare returned values with the actual project files, and validate the saved output with the downstream tool that will consume it.

sections.title: Structure can pass while the facts fail
paragraphs: The wrong answer has every required field and allowed type, but invents npm test and a deployment URL while omitting deployment_url from unknowns. The validator reports structure: valid and facts: rejected. A malformed object or missing field fails the structural gate; a missing source format is unverifiable.

This checker is intentionally limited to the fixture’s explicit Project, Check and Deployment lines. It is not a universal README or JSON Schema engine. JSONL belongs in report.cjs, where each line and lifecycle transition is checked. A complete stream and producer exit zero cannot turn a fabricated URL into a fact.

sections.title: A report file is evidence of output, not success
paragraphs: A saved output can still contain gaps. Inspect its source and decide whether the task passed. If a parser consumes the file, test an unknown value and a failed run first. This exercise creates local reports; it does not configure CI or schedules.

equivalence.summary: Claude text/json/stream-json output is replaced by Codex stdout/stderr behavior, JSONL events, output-last-message and output-schema with their distinct contracts.

quiz.explanation: A schema constrains fields and types. Facts still need reconciliation with the source and the task still needs verification.

lessons.title: Choose high-value, bounded CLI tasks
lessons.goal: Select a repeatable local task whose inputs, permissions and verification make scripted execution useful.
body: The strongest first CLI use case is a task with clear local inputs and an easy result check. Examples include summarizing documented setup, drafting release notes from a selected diff, identifying unsupported README claims or explaining a failing test log. These tasks reduce repetitive reading without requiring the agent to publish, change accounts or coordinate a complex external workflow. Start with a real recurring need, not with a desire to automate everything.

Choose an input boundary and output contract before running the agent. A release-note draft should name the exact diff or commit range. A log explanation should separate observed error messages from hypotheses. A small code fix should identify the failing behavior and the relevant test. A large prompt that simply says “improve the repository” lacks a stable basis for either safe execution or meaningful acceptance.

Repeatability requires more than a command that runs twice. Record the source version, working directory, client assumptions and validation method. If a report changes, you should be able to tell whether the source changed or the task was underspecified. For edits, preserve a baseline and inspect the final diff. For read-only analysis, compare the answer with the named inputs. Keep publication, scheduling and external communication as separate authorized actions.

mistakes: Automating a broad vague task before proving a small manual workflow works.

sections.title: A useful pipeline has an input and an acceptance rule
paragraphs: The batch has two explicit inputs, two distinct project names and two documented commands. verify-extraction.cjs accepts each current answer against its own source and rejects a crossed directory, fabricated claims, malformed JSON, missing fields and undocumented source. These results establish the offline consumer contract, not AI generation quality.

The provided synthetic log shows uppercase and padded-query failures. A grounded draft cites expected=2 actual=0 and proposes normalization as a hypothesis tied to notes.cjs; it does not announce a deployment outage or claim a fix ran. Use the app while exploring the task, then a one-shot pipeline after its inputs and check are stable.

sections.title: When to stay interactive
paragraphs: Stay interactive when exploring requirements or reviewing a visual result. Scripted execution fits a stable contract. Once the task works, package its repeatable guidance as a focused skill or reviewed script, keeping the uncertainty and verification requirements visible.
